name: Italian fascism
summary: Italian fascism, the movement and regime of Mussolini, holds that the nation is an ethical and spiritual whole created by and inseparable from the State, to which individuals, classes and private interests are subordinate. It rejects liberal democracy, Marxian socialism and pacifism in favour of rule by a single party and leader, class collaboration through state-supervised syndicates and corporations, war and expansion as signs of national vitality, a revived Roman heritage, and from 1938 a biological racism.
scope: The movement and regime of 1919-1943 as set out in Mussolini's 'Doctrine of Fascism' (1932), Alfredo Rocco's 1925 address endorsed by Mussolini, Gentile's 'Philosophic Basis of Fascism', Mussolini's speeches, the labour laws of 1926-34, the 1929 Lateran Treaty and the 1938 Manifesto of Race. The radical 1919 programme counts only where it stayed in force. Nazi biological racism as a system, later neo-fascist movements and the Salo Republic are excluded.

notes: Rules-7 pass. The earlier pass rested on Wikipedia pages; they are no longer evidence for any answer. Answers now rest on the full Doctrine of Fascism, Rocco's and Gentile's essays, Mussolini's speeches (1914-23), the 1926-34 labour statutes (ILO article), Britannica on the Lateran Treaty and the Italian regime, and the 1938 Manifesto of Race. Answers whose only support was a Wikipedia page were nulled unless a source now read settles them. Themes searched in the local corpora and on the web: economy and corporatism, property, strikes, parliament and elections, religion, race, women and family, empire and borders, education, press. Record sources for the regime after 1924 (economic policy such as the IRI and autarky, local government, population policy, colonial rule, women's rights, schooling) were looked for in Britannica pages that Britannica truncates behind a paywall, and the Fordham and Wikisource texts of the 1919 manifesto and 1927 Labour Charter could not be fetched, so those themes stay null.
